title: Tightest Range Touching Every List
statement:
You get k lists of integers. Each list is non-empty and sorted in non-decreasing order.

Find the range [a, b] (both ends included) that contains at least one number from every list and is as narrow as possible. Range [a, b] is narrower than [c, d] if b − a < d − c; if the widths are equal, the one with the smaller start wins. Return [a, b].

examples.why: 5, 8 and 9 fit in width 4. So do 8, 12 and 9 in [8, 12], but equal widths go to the smaller start.
One value is in every list, so the range can have width 0.
The second list forces a value of at least 10, and the first list cannot go above 3.

constraints: each list is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Suppose you have picked one number from each list. Which range covers them, and which pick should you change to have any chance of a narrower range?
The range is [smallest pick, largest pick]. Raising any pick other than the smallest can only keep or grow the range, so advance the list that holds the smallest pick.
Keep the current picks in a min-heap with a running maximum. Pop the minimum, record the range, push the next value from that list. Stop when some list runs out.

explain.intuition:
Hold one pointer per list, like merging k sorted lists. The current picks define a range from their minimum to their maximum. To make that range narrower, the only useful move is to raise the minimum: raising anything else cannot lower the maximum, and it does not lift the bottom either.

So repeatedly take the smallest pick, record the range it forms with the current maximum, and replace it with the next value of its own list. A min-heap finds the smallest pick fast, and a single variable tracks the maximum, since picks only grow. Once a list has no next value, its smallest element can no longer be raised, and no later range can be narrower than ones already seen.
steps: Push the first value of every list into a min-heap as (value, list, index). Let hi be the largest of them.
Pop the minimum lo. If hi − lo is narrower than the best range so far, record [lo, hi].
If that list has no next value, stop. Otherwise push its next value and update hi = max(hi, next).
Repeat, then return the best range.
pitfalls: Replacing the best range on equal width. The rule keeps the smaller start, and the first range found at a given width has the smallest start, so update only on strictly narrower.
Continuing after one list is exhausted. Without a value from that list a range is invalid.
Recomputing the maximum by scanning all picks each step. It only ever grows, so one variable is enough.

complexity.time: O(N log k), N = total values

solutions.title: Try every value as the left end
solutions.idea: For each value a, take the smallest value ≥ a from every list with binary search. The largest of those is the right end.

solutions.title: Min-heap of current picks
solutions.idea: Keep one pick per list in a min-heap and track the maximum. Always advance the list holding the minimum, since only that can narrow the range.

followups: Solve it by merging all values into one sorted array tagged with their list, then sliding a window that covers all k tags. How does it compare?
The lists are huge streams that do not fit in memory. Which version still works?
